Find the first positive zero positions in an observation plane at propagation distance \(z\).
questions.answer:
Model:
Apply the model for The Fraunhofer Diffraction Formula and Separable Apertures under every condition stated in the question; use SI units unless another unit is explicitly supplied.

Working:
Using \(\operatorname{sinc}(q)=\sin q/q\), the first zero of \(G\) obeys \(\pi a u=\pi\), so \(u=1/a\). Since \(u=x/(\lambda z)\), \[x_1=\frac{\lambda z}{a}.\] Likewise, \(v=1/b\) and \[y_1=\frac{\lambda z}{b}.\] Final result: the first positive zeros are \(x_1=\lambda z/a\) and \(y_1=\lambda z/b\); each aperture width controls the same coordinate in the pattern.

Final answer:
The first positive zeros are \(x_1=\lambda z/a\) and \(y_1=\lambda z/b\); each aperture width controls the same coordinate in the pattern.

Which direction has the narrower central diffraction feature, and why?
questions.answer:
Model:
Apply the model for The Fraunhofer Diffraction Formula and Separable Apertures under every condition stated in the question; use SI units unless another unit is explicitly supplied.

Equation \([5]\) separates the two directions. A wider \(x'\) factor has a transform \(G(u)\) compressed in \(u\), whereas the narrower \(y'\) factor has a broader \(H(v)\). Since \(x=\lambda z u\) and \(y=\lambda z v\), the same inverse scaling appears in the observation plane. Final result: the diffraction feature is narrower along \(x\), the direction corresponding to the wider aperture dimension \(x'\).

The diffraction feature is narrower along \(x\), the direction corresponding to the wider aperture dimension \(x'\).
